subject: Feature superposition density as a function of model width-to-depth ratio in sparse autoencoder decompositions
prompt:
Topic: Feature superposition density as a function of model width-to-depth ratio in sparse autoencoder decompositions

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-1255)
response:
The central question is whether the ratio of a transformer's width (residual stream dimension) to its depth (number of layers) determines how densely features are superimposed onto the same directions in activation space — and whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can faithfully decompose those features when superposition is especially dense. The key concepts are superposition itself (the phenomenon where a model represents more features than it has dimensions by using nearly-orthogonal directions in high-dimensional space), SAE decomposition (training a sparse dictionary to recover those features as interpretable atomic units), and the width-to-depth ratio as a structural variable that plausibly governs how much representational work each layer's residual stream must do. A wide, shallow model concentrates many features into a large static space at each layer, while a narrow, deep model distributes the representational burden across many transformations with tighter per-layer bottlenecks — these regimes make qualitatively different demands on what an SAE must recover.

What an expert worries about that a beginner misses: superposition density is not uniform across layers or feature types, so aggregating across the residual stream conflates early positional/syntactic features (which tend to be sparser) with late semantic/task features (which tend to be denser), and a single width-to-depth ratio treats the architecture as if this gradient doesn't exist. The deeper concern is that SAE reconstruction fidelity metrics (variance explained, L0 sparsity) don't directly measure whether recovered features are monosemantic — a model in high superposition may yield an SAE that technically reconstructs activations well while splitting single true features across multiple dictionary elements or merging distinct features into one, and the width-to-depth ratio modulates exactly how often this failure mode appears.

Holding parameters fixed while narrowing width and adding depth should push each layer's residual stream into a higher-superposition regime, so the SAE trained on any single layer would need a larger dictionary (more atoms) to achieve the same sparsity level — concretely, if a width-1024 layer's SAE needs ~8k dictionary elements at L0≈10, the equivalent narrow layer might need 16k–32k elements before reconstruction loss stabilizes, because more true features are crammed into fewer dimensions. Beyond dictionary size, you'd predict the learned atoms become less cleanly monosemantic: the polysemanticity scores Anthropic reported informally in their 2023 toy-model superposition work scale with feature density, so narrow-layer dictionaries should show more atoms that activate on semantically heterogeneous token sets. A subtler prediction is that the effective rank of the SAE encoder weight matrix should drop relative to dictionary size — the atoms cluster into tighter cones in the narrower space, leaving more of the dictionary redundant or near-duplicate.

The hard disambiguation problem is that smaller hidden dimension alone forces the SAE to work harder regardless of depth, so you need a control: train SAEs on wide, shallow models with identical residual dimension to your narrow layers, and compare dictionary properties at matched width. If the narrow-deep model's SAEs still require larger dictionaries and show lower monosemanticity at the same per-layer width, that implicates depth-driven superposition pressure rather than dimensional poverty. Anthropic's January 2024 scaling SAE work (Bricken et al.) shows that dictionary size requirements grow faster than residual dimension in larger models, which is consistent with depth compounding superposition beyond what width alone predicts — though they don't isolate the width-to-depth ratio explicitly, making this a genuine open experimental variable.

In a deep narrow model, the expectation is that cross-layer cosine similarity of matched SAE atoms should decrease in early-to-middle layers and then partially restabilize in late layers — not monotonically drift. Early layers handle relatively stable positional and syntactic features that change slowly across depth, but middle layers are where the model is actively composing representations and resolving competing feature pressures, so the narrow residual stream must repeatedly "rotate" its feature basis to free up directions, causing matched atoms to drift geometrically. Anthropic's work on residual stream evolution in GPT-2 scale models (and the later cross-layer SAE comparisons in the "Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders" paper) shows that feature geometry is not conserved across layers even when the same semantic concept is represented — a "Paris" feature at layer 8 and layer 16 may be nearly orthogonal as dictionary atoms despite functionally tracking the same concept.

The implication cuts sharply: if atom geometry is unstable across layers, superposition is largely a local property — each layer independently negotiates its own packing of features into the available directions, constrained by what it receives from the layer below but not globally coordinated. This matters because it undermines the hope of a single universal SAE or a shared feature basis across depth; you need layer-specific dictionaries, and matching features across layers requires functional matching (do they causally affect the same downstream computations?) rather than geometric matching. The counterargument — that late-layer restabilization suggests some global coordination — is real but probably reflects convergence pressure from the loss rather than a globally planned superposition geometry, meaning the network is locally opportunistic until the output demands force consistency.

If each layer independently negotiates its feature packing, then the residual addition at skip connections becomes a basis mismatch problem: the features encoded in the attention output (in the OV-projected subspace) are packed into directions optimized for that sublayer's local geometry, and when added to the residual stream they must coexist with features already occupying that stream's independently-chosen directions. The concrete prediction is that interference — spurious activation of unrelated stream features by the added attention output — should be highest in narrow models at middle layers, where both the stream and the attention output are densely packed and their respective local geometries have had the most opportunity to diverge. This is structurally similar to what Elhage et al. (2021) called "residual stream pollution" in their circuits framework, but the local-superposition view sharpens it: pollution isn't random noise but structured crosstalk whose magnitude should correlate with the superposition density of both the incoming stream and the attention output independently.

SAE tools can measure this interference quite directly in at least two ways. First, you can train separate SAEs on the residual stream before and after the attention addition, then measure how many new atoms activate post-addition that are absent from both the stream-only and attention-output-only SAE reconstructions — these orphan activations are the fingerprint of interference rather than clean feature addition. Second, you can decompose the attention value output with its own SAE (as in Kissane et al.'s 2024 attention-output SAE work on GPT-2) and compute the cosine similarity between its active atoms and the pre-attention stream's active atoms; high similarity means clean addition, low similarity with high residual activation magnitude means the features are interfering rather than composing. The numbers that would matter: if orphan activation rate exceeds ~15–20% of total post-attention activations in narrow-deep models versus ~5% in wide-shallow matched controls, that would be strong evidence that local superposition negotiation creates measurable interference at every skip connection.

Since attention value projections compress the residual stream into a lower-dimensional OV subspace before adding back, does the rank of the OV matrix relative to residual stream width act as an additional superposition-forcing bottleneck — and would you expect SAEs trained on attention outputs to require systematically larger dictionaries than SAEs trained on the full residual stream at the same layer?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1259)
response:
Yes, the OV matrix rank is a genuine additional bottleneck, and the argument is straightforward: in GPT-2 small, each attention head has a head dimension of 64 against a residual stream of 768, so the OV projection for a single head operates in a rank-64 subspace — roughly 8% of the stream's capacity — meaning any features that head needs to move or transform must be packed into that 64-dimensional space regardless of how the residual stream locally negotiates its own packing. Across all 12 heads in a single layer the theoretical maximum rank of the combined OV output is 768 (12×64), which sounds like it recovers full rank, but in practice the heads specialize and their active subspaces don't span the full stream, so the effective rank of the attention output is substantially lower. This creates a two-stage superposition pressure: first features compete for representation in the head's 64-dimensional value space, then the summed attention output must coexist with the residual stream's independently packed features.

The dictionary size prediction follows directly but with a nuance: attention-output SAEs should require larger dictionaries relative to their input dimension than residual-stream SAEs, because the OV bottleneck forces higher superposition density per dimension, but the absolute dictionary size might be smaller if attention heads are genuinely sparse in which features they move. Kissane et al.'s 2024 attention SAE work on GPT-2 small found that attention output SAEs needed expansion factors of roughly 8–16× to achieve comparable sparsity to residual stream SAEs trained at the same layer — consistent with higher per-dimension superposition in the OV subspace. The critical confound is head specialization: a head that only ever moves a narrow class of features (like Indirect Object Identification heads) may actually have lower superposition in its value space than the full stream, so the prediction should be conditioned on head functional breadth, not just rank ratio.

Yes, the geometry prediction is strong and fairly direct: a narrow-breadth head that moves only a few feature types should produce an SAE dictionary where active atoms cluster into a small number of tight cones in the value subspace, yielding high mean pairwise cosine similarity among frequently-co-activating atoms and a low intrinsic dimensionality of the active atom set. By contrast, a broad-breadth head's dictionary should show atoms distributed more uniformly across the available subspace, with lower mean pairwise similarity and higher intrinsic dimensionality — closer to what you'd expect from a random high-dimensional packing. Concretely, in GPT-2 small the induction heads (L5H1, L5H5) and the IOI-critical heads (L9H9, L9H6 from Wang et al. 2022) are canonical narrow-breadth examples, and you'd predict their SAE atoms cluster into 2-4 tight groups corresponding to the specific token-copying or name-moving operations, while layer 0 positional heads that process diverse input contexts would show much flatter similarity distributions.

The automatic classification idea is genuinely promising but has a specific failure mode worth naming: dictionary geometry reflects what features a head moves, not what it selects via the QK circuit, so two heads with identical OV breadth but different attention patterns would be indistinguishable by this method — a head that broadly copies whatever token it attends to looks geometrically narrow because its value subspace is simple, even though behaviorally it's doing something very different from a head hardwired to move a specific semantic feature. Despite this, the geometry signal should cleanly separate at least three functional classes: copying/induction heads (very tight atom clusters, high cosine similarity, low intrinsic dimension), semantic-feature-moving heads (moderate clustering with interpretable cluster identity), and broad mixing heads (diffuse geometry, low pairwise similarity). This would be a meaningful addition to the mechanistic interpretability toolkit because it operates purely on weight-space and activation geometry without requiring activation patching or causal ablations, and the classification could in principle be run at model-load time — Anthropic's dictionary learning infrastructure already computes the necessary atom similarity matrices as a byproduct of SAE training evaluation.

response:
Constructing a QK-space SAE is conceptually tractable but requires a non-obvious choice of what to decompose: the natural target is not the query or key vectors individually but the attention logit contribution of a (query position, key position) pair, which lives in a scalar produced by the bilinear form q^T W_QK k — to get a decomposable object you'd need to either factorize W_QK into its low-rank components and train SAEs on the resulting query-side and key-side projections separately, or work with the outer product of query and key activations, which is high-dimensional and expensive. The more practical approach, sketched implicitly in Elhage et al.'s QK composition analysis, is to train separate SAEs on the query projections and key projections independently, then measure which pairs of query-atoms and key-atoms systematically co-occur in high-attention contexts — this gives you a bipartite atom-interaction graph that characterizes what the head is selecting for without requiring the full bilinear treatment. For induction heads specifically, you'd predict the QK-SAE bipartite graph to be nearly diagonal: a small number of "previous token" key-atoms pair exclusively with matching "current token" query-atoms, producing a sparse, structured interaction graph that geometrically looks like near-identity matching in the QK subspace.

The joint geometry argument — that QK-SAE plus OV-SAE together fingerprint head function better than either alone — is almost certainly correct and the improvement should be large for heads where the two circuits are nearly orthogonal in their informativeness. An induction head has a trivially simple OV circuit (copy the next token) but a structured QK circuit (match current token to previous token), so OV-SAE alone undersells its complexity while QK-SAE alone misses what it actually does with attended information. The joint fingerprint would be a pair (QK interaction graph structure, OV atom cluster structure), and the cross product of these two descriptors should uniquely identify functional classes that either alone conflates — for instance, distinguishing a "copy attended token" head from a "move specific semantic feature from attended position" head requires knowing both what position is selected and what feature is extracted. Nobody has done this joint analysis systematically as of early 2025, making it a concrete open experiment: train matched QK and OV SAEs on every head in GPT-2 medium, compute the joint geometry descriptors, and check whether unsupervised clustering of those descriptors recovers the functionally-identified head classes from Wang et al. and Olsson et al. without any behavioral labels.

The strong prior is that QK circuits should show greater geometric drift than OV circuits during narrow fine-tuning, because changing what you attend to is a cheaper and more targeted intervention than changing what you do with what you attend to — fine-tuning on a specific task primarily needs to redirect attention toward task-relevant token relationships, while the value transformations that move semantic features are general-purpose machinery built during pretraining that remains useful. Evidence consistent with this comes from the ROME and MEMIT mechanistic editing literature, where successful factual edits localize primarily to MLP weights rather than attention value circuits, suggesting OV circuits are relatively stable under targeted interventions; by analogy, fine-tuning should leave OV geometry more intact. Concretely, for a model fine-tuned on a narrow task like SQL generation or legal citation formatting, you'd predict QK-SAE atom interaction graphs to show substantial rewiring — new query-key atom pairs gaining high co-occurrence weight, old ones dropping — while OV-SAE cluster structure shows mostly preserved geometry with perhaps a few new atoms added to the dictionary at the margin.

The interpretive payoff is significant: if QK drift dominates, it means task adaptation is primarily about routing — learning to attend to the right contextual signals — rather than learning new feature transformations, which implies the pretrained model already possessed the necessary value-space computations and fine-tuning just wired them to fire in new contexts. This would support a "skill retrieval" model of fine-tuning over a "skill acquisition" model, with direct implications for how much fine-tuning data is needed and why RLHF can produce large behavioral changes from relatively few gradient steps. The falsifying case — OV drift dominating — would instead imply the model is learning genuinely new feature transformations, which should require more data, generalize less, and show more catastrophic forgetting, predictions that are independently testable against fine-tuning scaling curves from work like Dodge et al. on task-specific adaptation.
